task.goal: Find why a school garden's manual rain gauge appears to undercount rainfall compared with a nearby public reading.
hard_constraints: Do not assume the public reading is ground truth for the garden's exact location.
No powered instruments, climbing, or changes to the public station.
Use only the existing gauge, a ruler, a marked cup and observations during the next three rain events; distinguish measurement error from local variation.
task.available_resources: Gauge, ruler, marked cup, site sketch and public daily rainfall report.
task.expected_result: A safe diagnostic sequence with uncertainty and a way to check each explanation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check the gauge’s collection and reading mechanism first
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether the gauge loses or misreports water before interpreting the public comparison. A wrong scale, leakage, retained water in a funnel, or a tilted gauge can produce low readings independently of rainfall differences.

Before the first event, sketch the location and inspect the gauge from ground level for cracks, debris, tilt and nearby obstructions. Identify whether it is a straight-sided vessel or a funnel-and-reservoir design: reservoir depth is not necessarily rainfall depth. Read the scale at eye level using the same meniscus convention each time.

Use the marked cup to add a known volume through the normal inlet. For a circular opening, measure its internal diameter with the ruler; expected rainfall depth in millimetres is 10 × volume in millilitres / opening area in square centimetres. This assumes a circular, measurable opening and adequate cup graduations. Check at two volumes and observe whether the level falls while standing. Drain afterward. If geometry or cup precision is inadequate, treat calibration as approximate.

During each of the next three events, keep the gauge in the same position, record its reading promptly after rain stops, note overflow or visible blockage, then empty it after recording. Match public reporting periods where possible. A demonstrated instrument defect supports measurement error; a sound calibration leaves exposure, reporting differences and genuine local rainfall variation unresolved.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: The smallest comparator is the expected depth from one known-volume pour versus the indicated depth. Repeat at a second volume: agreement weakens a scale-error explanation; a falling level supports leakage. During the three events, compare public and garden totals only over aligned intervals. Do not apply a precise correction unless the calibration discrepancy is repeatable and larger than ruler and cup uncertainty. Passing these checks does not establish that the public station received the same rainfall.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Test whether the garden location shields the gauge
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Investigate interception and wind exposure using an A–B–A placement sequence across the next three rain events. Leaves, walls and overhangs can intercept rain; turbulent wind can reduce collection. These effects can resemble genuinely lower rainfall at the garden.

Before starting, inspect the gauge for visible damage, check that its scale can be read consistently, and use a marked-cup pour to look for leakage. Record and empty the gauge afterward. Sketch the original position A and a safely accessible, more open position B within the garden. Use the ruler to check that the opening is level and record nearby obstruction directions. Avoid drip lines, splash zones and unstable supports. If no safe alternative position exists, this placement test is unavailable.

Measure event one at A, event two at B, and event three back at A. Keep reading and emptying procedures consistent. For each event, record garden rainfall, the public total for the corresponding reporting interval, observed wind direction, canopy dripping and whether rain appeared intermittent. The public record is a contextual comparator, not a reference standard.

A smaller garden-to-public deficit at B, followed by its return at A, is consistent with placement-related undercatch. Implementation needs only the existing items and moving the gauge between events. Its major limitation is that placement and storm conditions change together: three sequential events cannot conclusively separate exposure from spatial variation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the garden/public ratio at B with both A events, excluding zero-public totals and noting reporting mismatches. The simple comparator is the original placement. No improvement at B weakens the proposed exposure explanation, particularly if wind and rainfall character were similar. An improvement is suggestive rather than decisive because the storms were different. Visible interception or wind-linked deficits strengthen the explanation; inconsistent patterns leave local variation and exposure unresolved.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit time windows and water handling before comparing totals
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Check whether the apparent deficit comes from comparing different amounts of time. A public daily report may end at a different hour from the garden reading; a storm crossing that boundary can appear partly on another date. Delayed readings, evaporation, accidental emptying and overflow can also reduce the recorded garden total.

Before the next rain, inspect the gauge for damage and obvious obstructions, and check for leakage with a marked-cup pour. Record the result, then empty it. Read the public report’s stated accumulation interval if supplied. If it is absent, retain that uncertainty rather than assuming calendar-day totals.

Across the next three events, record when rain is observed to begin and end, when the gauge is read, every reading and every emptying. Read promptly after each event and, when safely practical, at the public reporting boundary. For rain continuing across a boundary, record the cumulative reading there; differences between successive readings give interval amounts if there has been no emptying or overflow. Never double-count an event reading and a boundary reading. Note near-capacity water levels and unusually long delays before reading.

Compare matched intervals and their combined total, including public days covering the same observed period. This requires someone available to make the observations; unavailable boundary readings limit the comparison. A discrepancy that disappears after matching windows supports an accounting explanation. A remaining discrepancy could reflect instrument error, exposure or real spatial variation; this method alone cannot choose among them.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the original same-date pairing with the reconstructed common-window totals for the three events. If individual daily deficits change into surpluses on adjacent dates while the combined discrepancy shrinks, timing is a plausible cause. If a deficit persists across fully aligned intervals with complete handling records, timing is weakened. If safe observation permits, compare an immediate post-rain reading with a later reading before emptying: a decline demonstrates post-collection loss, although evaporation and leakage may remain difficult to separate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use the marked cup as a simultaneous local rainfall comparator
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Collect the same rain in the existing gauge and the marked cup during each of the next three events. An independent collector beside the gauge can reveal whether the gauge reports less than another collector at the garden itself. Agreement between both collectors, despite disagreement with the public report, shifts attention toward shared exposure, reporting intervals or spatial rainfall variation.

This requires a cup that stands securely outdoors, has a measurable opening and retains rain without overflowing. Measure its internal opening diameter with the ruler if circular. Convert collected volume to rainfall depth: depth in millimetres = 10 × volume in millilitres / opening area in square centimetres. The cup’s volume markings must be sufficiently reliable; small catches may be below their useful resolution. If its opening geometry cannot be measured adequately, this method is unavailable.

Before each event, empty both vessels and place the cup near the gauge without either sheltering or splashing into the other. Choose stable, safely accessible positions away from obvious overhead interception and ground splash. Sketch their positions and note differences in rim height or exposure. Leave the gauge at its existing location. Observe only from safe shelter during rain; read both promptly afterward using consistent conventions. Record overflow, spilled water, debris and any handling uncertainty. Compare public totals only when accumulation windows match; otherwise retain that limitation.

The outcome changes through simultaneous independent collection, which avoids comparing different storms. It needs no extra equipment, but a household cup is an imperfect rain collector. Different aerodynamic shapes and rim heights can cause different catches. Three events can identify a repeatable collection discrepancy, but cannot establish the garden’s true rainfall precisely.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For each event, compare gauge depth with cup-derived depth, allowing for cup graduations and ruler uncertainty. A repeatably lower gauge reading beyond those uncertainties supports gauge-specific undercatch or reading error. Agreement weakens that explanation. If both are lower than aligned public totals, local variation remains plausible alongside shared exposure bias. Overflow or visibly different exposure invalidates that event’s comparison; do not count it as supporting evidence.

EXPAND.title: Check whether the public number represents the same quantity
EXPAND.proposal:
The apparent shortfall may arise when the public figure is interpreted: inches may be compared with millimetres, a multi-station area estimate may be treated as a point observation, or a displayed figure may represent a running total. This route tests the meaning of the comparator, a different issue from the earlier audit of reporting times.

A designated garden observer first inspects only the information supplied with the existing public daily report: units, station or area label, accumulation definition, and any indication that values are estimated or provisional. Do not obtain additional equipment or assume missing metadata. Check the garden gauge’s printed units as well. Convert inches to millimetres using 25.4 millimetres per inch when necessary. If the report represents an area, retain it as regional context rather than an expected garden measurement.

For the next three rain events, leave the gauge in its existing position, observe safely from ground level, record and empty it consistently, and compare only compatible quantities over matching periods where the report permits. Preserve both the original interpretation and the corrected interpretation so the effect is inspectable.

A documented unit or quantity mismatch can explain an apparent deficit without changing the gauge. An area estimate cannot establish rainfall at the garden. If the necessary definition is absent, stop the numerical attribution and report the garden measurement alongside an explicitly unidentified public comparator. This requires only the gauge, supplied report and observations; it does not diagnose leakage or exposure.
EXPAND.experiment: The observer bounds the trial to the next three events. Compare the original calculation with the calculation using documented units and quantity definitions. A reproducible conversion that removes the discrepancy supports an interpretation error; already compatible definitions falsify that explanation. Compared with the prior timing audit, this adds value only if semantic correction changes the conclusion. Stop if metadata are missing rather than spending observations reconstructing an unknowable figure. Record the shifted risk: a corrected comparison can still conceal gauge error or real spatial variation.

EXPAND.title: Use the marked cup to test simultaneous differences within the garden
EXPAND.proposal:
Actual rainfall reaching different parts of the garden may differ. A simultaneous second collector can test that possibility without treating the public station as truth or comparing different storms at different positions.

A designated observer first checks whether the existing marked cup can serve as an open collector: its mouth must have a measurable area, its graduations must measure volume, and it must stand securely without extra supports. For a circular mouth, measure the internal diameter with the ruler. Convert collected millilitres to rainfall millimetres as 10 × volume / mouth area in square centimetres. A tapered cup is acceptable because this uses volume and mouth area, not water depth. If the mouth area, graduations or stability are inadequate, stop this route.

Use the site sketch to choose two safely accessible, similarly open garden positions, avoiding overhead cover and obvious splash or drip sources. During event one, place the gauge and cup close together without either sheltering the other. This establishes whether their catches agree approximately. For event two, separate them between the two positions. For event three, exchange their positions. Empty before each event and read promptly afterward, only when safe. Note overflow, disturbance and observed wind; exclude affected comparisons.

A difference that follows position across the exchange, after approximate agreement when adjacent, supports a local difference in rainfall reaching collectors. A difference that follows the instrument supports collector bias. Neither pattern establishes the public station’s accuracy, and differing storm conditions or wind responses can leave attribution unresolved.
EXPAND.experiment: The first adjacent event is the smallest falsifying check: disagreement larger than cup and ruler uncertainty prevents treating the cup as an interchangeable comparator. If it passes, compare the two simultaneous position differences after exchanging collectors. Unlike the prior A–B–A route, each event supplies a concurrent comparison, although only two separated events limit confidence. Stop after three events or earlier if the cup is unstable, overflows or cannot resolve the catch. Compare diagnostic clarity with simply keeping the gauge fixed, while recording the added handling burden and risk of introducing a less reliable collector. A tiny or inconsistent positional difference provides no improvement and leaves broader spatial variation unresolved.

EXPAND.title: Gate calibration conclusions on measurement precision
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Check the gauge’s collection and reading mechanism first.” Preserve its ground-level inspection, known-volume pours, leakage observation and fixed-position monitoring, but add a decision rule before declaring the gauge accurate or applying a correction. The garden observer measures the inlet diameter in two directions and checks the cup’s smallest graduation. Use only a measurable inlet shape and pours large enough to resolve with the cup, without approaching gauge capacity. For a circular inlet, expected rainfall in millimetres is 10 × poured millilitres / inlet area in square centimetres. Calculate a plausible range using the ruler and cup reading uncertainty; an oval, inaccessible or poorly resolved inlet makes this calibration inconclusive.

Repeat each of two pour amounts after draining, using the normal inlet and consistent reading technique. A reproducible discrepancy outside the uncertainty range supports scale or transfer error; a visible decline after filling supports post-collection loss. Do not infer leakage from a decline too small to resolve or where evaporation remains plausible. Empty after testing.

For the next three rain events, keep the gauge fixed, read promptly when safe, record emptying and inspect for blockage, tilt, overflow and shielding. Compare with the public report only for compatible units and aligned periods. A calibration failure establishes a measurement problem but does not exclude local rainfall differences. Passing calibration leaves collection efficiency and local variation unresolved. If calibration prerequisites fail, retain raw readings explicitly as unvalidated; do not manufacture a correction. This adds a few dry pours compared with the source, but reduces the risk of correcting the gauge using a less precise cup.
EXPAND.experiment: The observer first performs one resolvable pour twice. Stop the calibration if inlet area cannot be measured adequately, the cup cannot resolve the amount, or results vary beyond estimated reading uncertainty. Otherwise complete the second-volume check. Apply a numerical scale correction only if a consistent proportional error explains both volumes within uncertainty; otherwise report the demonstrated defect without corrected rainfall totals. Over the three events, inspect whether an apparent garden deficit exceeds the calibration uncertainty. The smallest useful outcome is either a repeatable instrument discrepancy or an explicit finding that the available equipment cannot establish one; neither makes the public station ground truth.

EXPAND.title: Protect the timing audit from overflow and interrupted observations
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Audit time windows and water handling before comparing totals.” Preserve the inspection and marked-cup leakage check, public reporting-window audit, prompt event readings and accounting for every emptying. Close its operational gap: noting near-capacity readings alone does not preserve rainfall when a long event fills the gauge.

One garden observer owns the record for the next three rain events. Before rain, identify the gauge’s highest readable mark and choose a clearly readable lower mark as the intervention threshold. At observations that are already safely practical, if water reaches that threshold, record the amount, empty the gauge and add subsequent catches to the event total. Record intermediate readings without emptying as cumulative observations, not additional rainfall. No observation during unsafe weather is required.

If an observation is missed, continue from the water actually present. If overflow, an unexplained empty gauge or uncertain handling is observed or reasonably suspected, label that interval incomplete: its recorded catch is at most a lower bound, and its deficit cannot support a timing diagnosis. Resume a clean interval after recording and emptying. If the public boundary cannot be observed safely, use a longer comparison bounded by actual readings that match documented public boundaries; if none exists within the trial, present the totals separately.

Compare original same-date pairings with complete aligned intervals and their combined totals. A discrepancy that shrinks after alignment supports accounting error. A persistent deficit still permits instrument error, exposure or spatial variation. Compared with the source, this preserves otherwise lost measurable catch at the cost of occasional extra handling; each emptying also introduces transcription risk.
EXPAND.experiment: During the next three events, the observer uses the threshold rule only when a safe observation finds it reached. Stop numerical attribution for any interval with suspected overflow or an undocumented reset; retain its lower-bound catch and restart accounting. Check that each event total equals recorded emptied amounts plus the final remaining catch, with cumulative readings excluded from that sum. Then compare the original date pairing and the complete matched-window comparison. Adjacent-day compensation supports a timing explanation; a persistent discrepancy in complete windows weakens it. If no complete matched window survives, the bounded trial concludes that timing remains unresolved rather than attributing missing water to local rainfall.
